openers.pol: Some of the costliest things an economy makes are never sold. Microscopic particles drift through city air, acidic rain falls on forests and lakes, and everyday rubbish needs somewhere to go. Breathing fine particles is linked to disease throughout the body and to large numbers of early deaths. This part of the course follows those unwanted by-products and the tools societies use to limit them. It begins with the harm itself, and with the ways economists try to put a money value on the damage an environmental change causes.
openers.pollution-economics-and-environmental-he: Pollution is what happens when the costs of making and using things spill onto people who never agreed to bear them. Particles too small to see drift through the air, and rain turns unusually acidic. Waste piles up as household rubbish, as dangerous chemical leftovers, and as old factory land left behind. Some contamination has no single source at all, gathering in small amounts from whole landscapes. This chapter looks at each of these harms in turn, what they do to health and ecosystems, and what has worked to reduce them.

reviews.pollution-economics-and-environmental-he: Pollution takes many forms, but the same pattern runs through this chapter. Fine particles that reach deep into the lungs are the leading environmental risk factor for early death, while acid rain, landfill gas and leachate, hazardous waste and diffuse farm runoff each damage air, water and soil in their own way. The burdens fall hardest on poorer people and minorities who live near polluting sites. Yet policy works: US emissions of the main pollutants fell 79% after 1970, EU deaths from PM2.5 fell 57%, and scrubbers, treaties and emissions trading cut acid rain. Economists weigh such choices with damage functions, though critics warn these miss major risks.

nature-pol-068.title: Particulate matter: the most dangerous thing in the air
nature-pol-068.text: No level of exposure is safe. Particulate matter is the name for microscopic solid or liquid particles suspended in the air, and it is considered the most dangerous form of {{ref:nature-found-055}}. A mix of particles and air is called an aerosol. The particles come from both natural and human sources. Some are wind-blown mineral dust and sea salt. Others are organic matter, or form in the air from gases such as sulfur dioxide (SO2) and ammonia. The danger lies in how far they travel inside the body. Particles reach deep into the lungs and then ride the blood to organs such as the brain. Airborne particulate matter is classed as a Group 1 carcinogen, a substance known to cause cancer. Fine particles, called PM2.5 ({{ref:nature-found-073}}), are the leading environmental risk factor for early death worldwide. Yet this is also a hopeful story. Because so many sources are human, the risk is one that policy can reduce, and many countries now set standards for it. After the United States passed its {{ref:nature-pol-153}} of 1970, combined emissions of the main regulated pollutants and the gases that form them fell 79% between 1970 and 2024.

nature-pol-046.title: Acid rain: when burning coal sours the sky
nature-pol-046.text: In 1852, in industrial Manchester, Robert Angus Smith first linked acid rain to air pollution. Acid rain is rain, snow or other precipitation that is unusually acidic. Acidity is measured on the pH scale, where lower numbers mean more acid. Most water sits between 6.5 and 8.5, while acid rain averages about 4–5; one definition draws the line below 5. The acid starts as gas. Burning fuels and smelting ores release sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, which reactions in the air turn into sulfuric and nitric acid. Humans now dominate the supply, upsetting the natural {{ref:nature-eco-273}}. Fossil fuels and industry emit 70 Tg (teragrams) of sulfur a year as SO2, far more than wildfires (2.8 Tg) and volcanoes (7–8 Tg) combined. Power plants alone produce two-thirds of the sulfur dioxide in the air and a quarter of the nitrogen oxides. Coal-fired stations, animal farming, fertilizers, steel mills and vehicles all contribute. The worst-hit regions run from eastern Europe into Scandinavia, across the eastern third of the United States and into southeastern Canada.

nature-pol-064.title: Municipal solid waste: what a city throws away
nature-pol-064.text: What a city throws away says a lot about it. Municipal solid waste is everyday rubbish: the trash or garbage of items thrown out by the public. Most definitions leave out industrial, agricultural, medical and radioactive waste, and sewage sludge. Its make-up varies greatly between places and over time. Typical Chinese municipal waste is 55.9% food residue, 11.2% plastics and 8.5% paper. Where recycling is well developed, what is left is mainly plastic film and packaging that cannot be recycled. The industry that handles it has four parts: recycling, composting, disposal and burning waste to make energy. Waste hierarchies rank these methods from most to least preferred. Reducing and reusing come first, then recycling or composting, then recovering energy, and only last treatment and disposal. The ranking matters for the climate too. Municipal waste produces large amounts of methane, and nearly 90% of it could be avoided with existing technologies.

nature-pol-058.title: Landfill: burying the rubbish, and the costs
nature-pol-058.text: Burying rubbish is the oldest and most common way to get rid of it. A landfill is a site for disposing of waste, including household rubbish ({{ref:nature-pol-064}}). Yet systematic burial, with daily and final covers over the waste, only began in the 1940s. The modern sanitary landfill followed. It is an engineered facility that separates and confines waste, and it was widely adopted in the 1960s and 1970s to end open dumps. Landfills still carry costs. They take up much land and can contaminate groundwater and soil. Neighbors put up with dust, odor, noise, and disease-carrying rats and flies, and local property values fall. Permitting a new US landfill generally takes five to seven years and costs millions of dollars. When a site closes, it often gets a second life as a park, a bike course or a solar farm.

nature-pol-054.title: Hazardous waste: rubbish that stays dangerous
nature-pol-054.text: Some rubbish stays dangerous long after it is thrown away. Hazardous waste is waste that can damage human health or the environment. It earns that label in one of four ways: it is toxic, reactive, corrosive or ignitable. As of 2022, humanity produced 300–500 million metric tons of it a year. The sources are surprisingly ordinary. Solvents, batteries and the by-products of metal refining are common ones. So are dry cleaners, car repair shops, hospitals and photo labs. Handled badly, this waste becomes {{ref:nature-found-079}} of the worst kind. It fouls the air, raising illness and death, and contaminates groundwater and soil. That is why it is regulated at local, national and international levels.

nature-pol-075.title: Nonpoint source pollution: contamination with no address
nature-pol-075.text: A single factory pipe is easy to find. A thousand fertilized fields are not. Nonpoint source pollution is diffuse contamination of water or air that does not come from one identifiable source. It is often the combined effect of small amounts of pollutants gathered from a large area. It contrasts with {{ref:nature-pol-170}}, which comes from a single source. Nonpoint pollution travels by {{ref:nature-eco-275}}, rain, deposition from the air, drainage and seepage, which makes it hard to trace back. Paved city surfaces and farms that spread fertilizer and manure are major sources. Even a smokestack, a single source where it stands, acts as nonpoint where its pollution lands after being carried far and mixed with others. In the United States it is the leading cause of water pollution, mainly from farm runoff and altered waterways.

nature-pol-050.title: Brownfield land: the polluted leftovers of industry
nature-pol-050.text: The word was first used on June 28, 1992, at a US congressional field hearing. Brownfield land is previously developed land, abandoned or underused, that may be polluted from past industrial use. Countries define it differently, mainly over whether contamination must actually be present. Examples include abandoned factories, ash ponds, old landfills, dry cleaners and gas stations. Their ground may hold spilled hydrocarbons, solvents, pesticides, asbestos and heavy metals such as lead. The United States alone is estimated to have over 500,000 brownfield sites contaminated below the level that triggers {{ref:nature-pol-176}}. Not all of this land is dead ground. Industrial brownfields can be valuable ecosystems that support rare plants, animals and invertebrates. Redeveloping them has become a key part of large urban greening projects.

nature-pol-070.title: How breathing particles shortens lives
nature-pol-070.text: In 2023, fine particles in the air contributed to 7.9 million deaths worldwide. Of these, 4.9 million were linked to outdoor air pollution and 2.8 million to household air pollution. Breathing {{ref:nature-pol-068}} is linked to disease throughout the body. It contributes to stroke, heart disease, respiratory disease, many cancers, preterm birth and cognitive impairment. Both short bursts and long years of exposure cause harm. Scientists first showed the link to premature deaths in the early 1970s, and the 1993 Harvard Six Cities study established it firmly for cities. Policy can bend these numbers. In the EU, deaths from PM2.5 fell 57% between 2005 and 2023, as policies cut primary emissions, the particles released directly, by 38%. China's 2013 air pollution action plan cut average PM2.5 by a third by 2017, and fewer people died.

nature-pol-048.title: What acid rain does to lakes, forests and stone
nature-pol-048.text: Below a pH of 5, most fish eggs will not hatch. Below 4, adult fish die. {{ref:nature-pol-046}} harms forests, fresh waters and soils, kills plants and animals, damages buildings and affects human health. In lakes and streams, lower pH comes with more aluminum in the water, which harms fish, other aquatic animals, microbes and plants. In soil, acid kills sensitive microbes and disables their enzymes, so functions such as decomposition collapse. High-altitude forests suffer most, because the clouds and fog around them are more acidic than rain. Cities feel it too. Acids react with limestone and marble in buildings and statues to form gypsum, which flakes off. And breathing the pollutants linked to acid rain, such as nitrogen dioxide, can damage the airways.

nature-clim-234.title: Damage functions: pricing each degree of warming
nature-clim-234.text: How much does one more degree of warming cost? A damage function is the economist's answer: a relationship, used in {{ref:nature-val-001}}, that estimates the economic damage caused by an environmental change such as warming. Researchers have built them for rising seas, farm productivity and the effect of heat on how much work people get done. A common base form makes damages grow with the square of warming. So 2 °C causes 4 times the damage of 1 °C, and 3 °C causes 9 times. Some versions add tipping points, so damages speed up, or jump, once warming passes 2-3 °C. Estimates of the {{ref:nature-clim-241}}, the money value of harm from each extra unit of emissions, are highly sensitive to the damage function chosen, along with the discount rate. A 2020 paper using an updated function found that around 2 °C of warming would be 'optimal' in one leading climate-economy model, DICE. Critics such as {{ref:nature-hist-045}} argue that standard damage functions miss many of society's most important risks. The argument is far from settled.

nature-pol-073.title: How airborne particles cool and cloud the planet
nature-pol-073.text: Particles in the air do not only harm lungs; they also change the climate. Aerosols alter how much incoming sunlight and outgoing heat Earth keeps. They act directly, by scattering and absorbing radiation, and indirectly, by changing clouds, since cloud droplets form on particles. Not all particles behave alike. Soot absorbs radiation strongly, while sea-salt particles only scatter it. Overall, the direct effect is a negative {{ref:nature-eco-004}}, which means cooling. Aerosol effects remain the biggest source of uncertainty in climate predictions.

nature-pol-069.title: Coarse, fine and ultrafine: sorting particles by size
nature-pol-069.text: Size decides how deep a particle gets, and so how much harm it can do. Scientists group particles by diameter. Coarse PM10 particles measure 10 micrometers or less, and fine PM2.5 particles 2.5 micrometers or less. Ultrafine particles are smaller still. A micrometer is a thousandth of a millimeter. Coarse particles lodge in the nose, throat and upper airways. Fine ones penetrate deep into the lungs, reaching the smallest airways and air sacs. That is why, across all causes of death, PM2.5 has more severe effects than PM10.

nature-pol-074.title: Filters, scrubbers and charged plates that catch dust
nature-pol-074.text: Much of the dust a factory makes never leaves the building. In most industrialized countries particle emissions are highly regulated, and industries meet the rules with dust collection systems. These include cyclones, fabric filters, wet scrubbers and electrostatic precipitators, all forms of {{ref:nature-found-082}}. Fabric filters, also called baghouses, are the most common in general industry. Electrostatic precipitators work differently. They give particles an electric charge and collect them on large charged plates.

nature-pol-072.title: Who breathes the dirtiest air
nature-pol-072.text: Particle pollution does not fall evenly. Its burden lands more heavily on non-White people and on those living in poverty. Living near facilities that emit particles raises PM2.5 exposure and rates of illness and death. About 1.6 billion people live near sources of PM2.5 and other toxins, and 900 million of them live near super-emitting facilities. In the United States, the gap for Black people is larger than income alone explains, and scholars link it to housing segregation. The pattern repeats the wider story of {{ref:nature-found-058}}.

nature-pol-071.title: The WHO's limits for safe air
nature-pol-071.text: By the World Health Organization's yardstick, 97% of the world's population breathes unsafe air. The WHO sets guideline limits for particle exposure, above which health risks rise. For PM2.5, the yearly average should not exceed 5 μg/m3, and the 24-hour average 15 μg/m3. For PM10, the limits are 15 μg/m3 a year and 45 μg/m3 over 24 hours. The unit means micrograms of particles in each cubic meter of air. The 97% figure comes from the 2021 guideline for PM2.5.

nature-pol-047.title: Acid deposition: wet and dry routes to the ground
nature-pol-047.text: Acid does not need rain to fall. Acid deposition is the delivery of acids from the air to the ground, by two routes. Wet deposition happens when rain, snow or fog carries acids down to the surface. Dry deposition happens when particles and gases simply stick to the ground, plants or other surfaces. That quieter route matters. Dry deposition can make up 20 to 60% of total acid deposition, so {{ref:nature-pol-046}} tells only part of the story.

nature-pol-049.title: How scrubbers, treaties and trading tamed acid rain
nature-pol-049.text: Acid rain has been cut back in three ways. The first is technical. Scrubbing sulfur from power-station exhaust, called flue-gas desulfurization, removes 95% or more of the SO2 from a typical coal-fired station. The second is diplomatic. Under the 1979 {{ref:nature-gov-132}}, sulfur and particle emissions have fallen 30-80% in Europe and 30-40% in North America since 1990. The third is economic: {{ref:nature-pol-253}}. Each polluter holds allowances, permits for its emissions, and can sell the ones it no longer needs after installing controls. The first such market came with the 1990 amendments to the US {{ref:nature-pol-153}}, to cut SO2 at the lowest cost to society.

nature-pol-063.title: Alternatives to burying waste
nature-pol-063.text: Burying waste is not the only option, and not always the cheapest. Alternatives to {{ref:nature-pol-058}} include cutting waste and recycling, burning it to make energy, composting, and anaerobic digestion, in which microbes break waste down without oxygen. Depending on local economics and incentives, these can be made cheaper than landfilling. Some governments push hard. Germany, Austria, Sweden, Denmark, Belgium, the Netherlands and Switzerland have banned landfilling untreated waste. The UK taxes biodegradable waste sent to landfill, and England set up a scheme for councils to trade landfill quotas. The idea of {{ref:nature-eecon-057}} aims to shrink landfill volume as far as possible.

nature-pol-061.title: Landfill gas: methane from buried rubbish
nature-pol-061.text: Landfills are the third largest emitter of methane worldwide. Landfill gas is the mix produced when microbes digest buried organic waste without oxygen. On average it is about half methane and slightly less than half carbon dioxide, which links landfills to {{ref:nature-eco-201}}. Well-managed landfills collect the gas, then either burn it off in a flare or use it to generate electricity. More than 850 US landfills recover it. Capturing landfill methane is also a common kind of project for carbon offsets, schemes in which one party pays to cut emissions to make up for its own.

nature-pol-060.title: Leachate: the poisoned liquid under a landfill
nature-pol-060.text: Rain that falls on a landfill does not stay clean. Leachate is the contaminated liquid formed when water seeps through the waste, picking up organic matter, heavy metals and other pollutants. If it escapes, it can contaminate groundwater. Modern landfills fight back with impermeable liners several meters thick, stable sites and systems that collect the liquid. When a landfill is full, it is sealed to keep rain out, so no new leachate forms.

nature-pol-062.title: Landfill aftercare: a cost that may never end
nature-pol-062.text: A landfill's costs do not stop when it closes. Aftercare is the long period after a site is full and capped, when liners, gas capture ({{ref:nature-pol-061}}) and treatment of leachate ({{ref:nature-pol-060}}) keep limiting harm. It may last several decades, or forever. Sealed waste keeps its power to pollute, so replacing liners and treating leachate is an indefinite requirement. In the Netherlands, aftercare can cost more than 20 million euros per landfill.

nature-pol-059.title: Inside a landfill: the slow life of buried waste
nature-pol-059.text: A sealed landfill is less a tomb than a slow digester. A sanitary landfill works as a biological reactor, in which microbes break organic waste into simpler, less toxic compounds over several phases. First, oxygen trapped in the waste feeds aerobic breakdown until the microbes use it up. The rest of the work happens without oxygen ({{ref:nature-eco-213}}). In the acid phase, fatty acids build up and the leachate's pH falls from about 7.5 to 5.6. In the longest phase, methane-making microbes turn the acids into methane and carbon dioxide. Finally methane production almost stops, as nutrients run short and oxygen seeps back in.

nature-pol-066.title: Reuse: keeping things in service
nature-pol-066.text: The greenest item is often the one already made. Reuse means using things again, by repairing, gifting, refurbishing or lending them, instead of throwing them away. It lengthens product life and reduces the need for fresh raw materials. Unlike recycling, it does not break items down into raw materials, which saves time, money, energy and resources. That makes extending an item's use the least energy-intensive option, preferable to recycling or disposal. Online networks such as Freecycle list unwanted items for others to take, keeping them out of landfills.

nature-pol-065.title: Source separation: sorting waste where it starts
nature-pol-065.text: Sorting rubbish at home makes everything downstream easier. Source separation means sorting waste into types, such as biodegradable, recyclable, residual and hazardous, where it is produced. It improves recycling, prevents contamination, allows composting and ensures hazardous waste is properly treated. Separated and mixed wastes then go to materials recovery facilities, which sort them by hand and with screens, magnets and optical sorting. Separating, composting and recycling together can also cut methane emissions from municipal waste.

nature-pol-067.title: Waste-to-energy: power from rubbish
nature-pol-067.text: Rubbish can keep the lights on. Waste-to-energy is generating power from municipal waste, by burning it, by capturing landfill gas, or through pyrolysis or gasification, which break waste down with heat. Older incinerators emitted many pollutants. New rules and technology changed that. US rules in 1995 and 2000 cut dioxin emissions from such plants by over 99% below 1990 levels, and mercury by over 90%. Because waste contains food, wood and paper, burning it can partly count as bioenergy, energy made from living material.

nature-pol-055.title: Disposing of hazardous waste: bury, burn or recycle
nature-pol-055.text: Dangerous waste has three main exits: secure landfills, fire and recycling. For landfilling, it is first treated and stabilized, and the landfill needs barriers along its foundations to stop groundwater contamination. Incinerators burn it at 870–1400 °C, greatly shrinking it, but the leftover ash and gases can be hazardous too. Some materials, such as lead–acid batteries and circuit boards, can be recycled into new products. At the extreme, plasma treatment above 3000 °C turns waste into inert, rock-like slag. It is very expensive, but it suits persistent pollutants such as PCBs.

nature-pol-057.title: Exporting poison: the trade in hazardous waste
nature-pol-057.text: When disposal got expensive at home, the waste went abroad. As laws such as the US RCRA raised disposal costs in developed nations in the 1970s, shipments of {{ref:nature-pol-054}} to poorer countries with weaker rules grew fast. In 1990, OECD countries, a club of mostly rich nations, exported around 1.8 million tons of it. The 1992 {{ref:nature-gov-129}}, signed by 199 countries, set out to stop this flow. The aim lives on in the UN's global goals, where Goal 12 includes sound management of chemicals and wastes throughout their life cycle.

nature-pol-056.title: Who lives next to hazardous waste
nature-pol-056.text: Hazardous waste does not land at random. Poorer people and social minorities face a higher risk of exposure to it and its pollution. An Austrian study found that people living near industrial sites are more often unemployed and less educated, and twice as likely to be immigrants. Groups who rely on local land and streams for food and water, including Native Americans, face multiplied risk.

nature-pol-077.title: Slowing the runoff: controlling diffuse pollution
nature-pol-077.text: Stopping diffuse pollution mostly means slowing water down. {{ref:nature-pol-075}} is controlled by land practices that slow runoff and trap pollutants before they reach water. Grass buffer strips between paved areas and streams let soil absorb pollutants first. Retention ponds hold storm runoff so contaminants settle out and stay trapped. Farmers use contour plowing, mulching, rotating crops, perennial crops and plowing less. They also leave strips of vegetation along waterways ({{ref:nature-nbs-260}}). Mixing trees with farming ({{ref:nature-nbs-247}}) can also clean the air by absorbing pollutants such as particulate matter.

nature-pol-078.title: Why diffuse pollution escapes the regulators
nature-pol-078.text: A permit needs a pipe to attach to. Nonpoint pollution has no single discharge point, so it is hard to regulate, and US federal law leaves it largely to states and voluntary programs. For that reason, diffuse sources were excluded from the permit program of the {{ref:nature-pol-155}}. State programs rely instead on best management practices, seeking the least costly way to cut the most pollution. Since 1987, federal grants under section 319 of that law have funded these state programs. The results are weak. A 2015 article found the law effective for single-source discharges but not for diffuse ones.

nature-pol-076.title: Sediment, nutrients, toxins and germs in runoff
nature-pol-076.text: Four kinds of pollutant dominate runoff: sediment, nutrients, toxic chemicals and disease-causing pathogens. Sediment clouds water, cutting light for underwater plants and for the fish and shellfish that depend on them. Of the nutrients, phosphorus and nitrogen cause the most concern. The toxic chemicals include heavy metals and compounds such as PCBs and DDT, which resist breakdown and persist in the environment. For pathogens, coliform bacteria in runoff serve as an indicator of water pollution rather than as a cause of disease.

nature-pol-052.title: Why polluted land sits empty for decades
nature-pol-052.text: Some contaminated land sits unused for decades for a simple reason: cleaning it would cost more than the land would then be worth. Brownfields also carry an environmental stigma that can delay redevelopment. The US {{ref:nature-pol-176}} law has been criticized for pushing investment to greenfields, undeveloped land, through severe no-fault liability, which makes owners pay whether or not they caused the pollution. Redevelopment grew in the 2000s as developable land became scarcer in crowded areas. Governments help too. The federal Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) awarded nearly 1,000 cleanup grants worth almost $190 million from 2002 through 2013, and cleanup costs are fully tax-deductible.

nature-pol-053.title: Cleaning up brownfields
nature-pol-053.text: Poisoned ground can be healed, though rarely by one method alone. Brownfield remediation is cleaning contaminated former industrial land so it can be reused. Techniques include heating soil in place, bioremediation, which uses living organisms to break pollutants down, oxidizing contaminants in place, and soil vapor extraction, which draws out polluting gases. They are often combined. Binders can be mixed into soil to stop chemicals leaching out. In phytoremediation, deep-rooted plants draw heavy metals out of the soil.

nature-pol-051.title: What is a polluted plot worth?
nature-pol-051.text: Contamination scrambles the usual sums of property. Valuing a brownfield needs specialized appraisal, because pollution changes a site's best use and its value both before and after cleanup. The value should allow for lingering stigma and possible liability to third parties. Normal appraisal often fails, so appraisers turn to {{ref:nature-val-085}}, case studies or statistical analysis. The payoff from cleanup can be large. A 2014 study looked at EPA cleanup grants from 2002 through 2008. It found an average benefit of almost $4 million per site, and a median, or middle value, of $2.1 million. Some environmental firms team up with insurers to guarantee cleanup costs.
